title: Tasmanian football club coach charged with rape
text:
A former northern Tasmanian football coach has been charged with three counts of rape, leading to the resignation of the football club's president.

Police confirmed a 44-year-old man from northern Tasmania had been charged with the offences that were alleged to have occurred in April last year.

The man is believed to be former Bracknell football coach, Josh Adams.

He is scheduled to appear in the Launceston Magistrates Court early next year.

In a statement, Northern Tasmanian Football Association (NTFA) president Peter Gutwein said the association had recently been informed that a coach had been charged with "a serious criminal offence".

But he said the NTFA would not provide further comment as the matter was now before the courts.

News of charges being laid against Adams were first published by an independent media outlet.

Its reporting detailed private messages exchanged between Bracknell Football Club president Nicole Jones and the mother of Adams's alleged victim

Yesterday, Ms Jones announced via social media that she would be "standing down as president and all official club duties with immediate effect".

"I acknowledge that what I said [in the messages] was disrespectful, inappropriate and wrong, and I unreservedly apologise for these comments," she said.

In his statement, Mr Gutwein said the league was "deeply concerned" by the content of the private messages.

"The NTFA has referred the matter to the AFL for independent consideration and acknowledges that the President has unreservedly apologised for those comments and stood aside from all official club duties with immediate effect," he said.

"The NTFA recognises that individuals who report allegations of sexual violence must be treated with dignity, compassion and respect."

Adams had not re-committed to coaching Bracknell as of last month.

It is understood he has since been stood down from the role, and will be replaced.

title: Former Port Adelaide AFL player Daniel Stewart dies at 37
text:
The Port Adelaide AFL club has said it will honour Daniel Stewart at the first home game of 2027 after the former Power forward's death at the age of 37.

Stewart, who played 36 games and kicked 31 goals for Port Adelaide between 2010 and 2013, died suddenly yesterday.

The tall key forward was drafted by the Power in the 2009 rookie draft and promoted to the senior list at the end of that season.

Originally from Victoria, Stewart was recruited from SANFL team North Adelaide after playing for the Eastern Ranges and AFL Queensland club Labrador.

His best AFL return came in the final round of 2010 at Docklands against Richmond, where Stewart kicked four goals in a 10-point win for the Power.

"On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel's family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh," Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said in a statement.

"We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.

"Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.

"The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel's passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him."

The club stated it would honour Stewart by wearing black armbands at their first home game at Adelaide Oval next season.

title: Elon Musk has a lot to lose at US midterms as pollsters tip blue wave
text:
Last November, Elon Musk was looking to step away from the halls of power.

"You know, I've generally found that when I get involved in politics, it ends up badly," he told investor and YouTuber Nikhil Kamath.

"Best to avoid where possible."

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive's stint as a special government employee leading the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ended months earlier after a string of controversies.

Mr Musk also quietly shelved plans to launch a political party, which had been announced during a short-lived feud with US President Donald Trump.

But as the country's midterm elections approach, Mr Musk is making another foray into politicking.

And with control of Congress now in reach for Democrats, the stakes for the trillionaire are higher than ever.

Trying to turn back a blue tide

With Mr Trump's approval rating at record lows, Democrats are banking on breakthrough performances at the November 3 elections.

Forecasters say the House of Representatives is all but guaranteed to flip blue, while the Senate result is, at the least, a toss-up.

Why Musk is spending millions to get Trump elected Elon Musk has promised to give away $US1 million a day leading up to the United States presidential election

Despite arguing that "they never poll us right", the president has embarked on a campaign blitz across the country.

He has also promised to pay every American adult $US5,000 (about $7,100) if Republicans retain control of Congress, reminiscent of the $US5,000 cheques cut from DOGE savings once floated in early 2025.

Mr Musk may be staying off the campaign trail, but behind the scenes, he has become the biggest known midterm donor, sinking about $US442 million into Republican groups in this election cycle.

At least $US158 million of that has gone toward a race in his home state of Texas, in which Republicans are at risk of losing a once-safe US Senate seat to Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Mr Talarico's campaign has released ads claiming Mr Musk wants to "buy his own US senator" by bankrolling Republican candidate Ken Paxton.

"So let's remind Elon: Texas is not for sale," the ads say.

Separately, Mr Musk earlier this month said he would give a SpaceX share to "every child in America" in 2027. While he did not provide details of the giveaway, Mr Trump claimed it as a victory for his Trump accounts program, through which he said the stock would be distributed.

Dems put target on Musk's back

There is a lot at stake for Mr Musk if control of the House changes over.

Democrats have been calling for investigations into several areas of his dealings, and if they win back gavels in several congressional committees, they will have the power to follow through.

Mr Musk recently landed himself in Democrats' sights after Ukraine reported its access to the SpaceX owned Starlink and Starshield services had been restricted, affecting the country's ability to defend against Russian drone attacks.

Starlink slowdown in Ukraine Ukraine says people will die as a result of throttled Starlink services in the country. Here's how its armed forces rely on the crucial service.

In response to the matter, Mr Musk said Starshield's systems were controlled by the US government.

Mr Trump and the SpaceX owner have denied responsibility, but a Wall Street Journal report cited officials and people familiar with the matter as saying Mr Musk ordered the throttled speeds.

Days prior, Mr Musk commented that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "gone too far" by striking Russian oil refineries.

Both Donald Trump Elon Musk say they were not involved in restrictions to Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield access. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, told Politico the incident raised questions about Mr Musk's power.

"What happens when one guy gets a giant contract from the government and then uses it to do something that shuts down communication in a war that has been extremely important to the United States to support Ukraine?" she said.

"There's a lot of different parts of the corruption around Musk."

Elon Musk's DOGE agency explained There has been an escalation in the legal battles over billionaire Elon Musk's new US government efficiency agency. Here's what we know about DOGE.

Democrats on several committees have also earmarked DOGE for congressional scrutiny.

Through its 10-month lifespan, the department cut an estimated 250,000 federal jobs, allegedly accessed sensitive data, and withheld congressionally appropriated funds.

Democrats have also alleged conflicts of interest between Mr Musk and the federal government.

Republicans blocked previous attempts by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform to subpoena Mr Musk.

"There's any number of House committees that would have jurisdiction in some respect over him," said Harry Melkonian, an honorary associate at the United States Studies Centre.

"He's a major defence contractor and NASA contractor, so his companies receive staggering amounts of federal money each year."

Democrats would be able to call congressional investigations into Elon Musk if they win back the House. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

In June 2025, representative Jasmine Crockett, who sits on the oversight committee, vowed to "bring Elon Musk in" once Democrats regained the majority.

"And we can have him under oath, and we can have him tell us about everything that he did," she said in an appearance on MSNBC.

In response to the Politico report that Democrats were discussing possible investigations into Mr Musk, the trillionaire threatened to retaliate against congressional investigations.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword," he wrote on X.

"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

Testimonies, document production

Mr Musk could be called to testify at committee hearings and required to produce documents under a congressional investigation.

"For somebody like Musk, it would be truly awful to be sitting for eight hours a day, having a panel of people just questioning everything you do," Dr Melkonian said.

"It becomes television news … and he is a businessman selling consumer products."

Elon Musk switches focus back to Tesla. Is it too late? Experts say it could be too late for Tesla to "separate the man from the machine" as Elon Musk's personal brand hits an all-time low.

But refusing to cooperate would present its own problems.

"On the political side, as a major contractor, he would be reluctant to antagonise a congressional majority because his companies depend on money voted by Congress," Dr Melkonian said.

"Legally, he could be held in contempt of Congress."

The federal misdemeanour is punishable by imprisonment of up to 12 months.

If an investigation uncovers any wrongdoing, the findings can be referred to the Department of Justice for prosecution.

The US attorney would be bound to take the matter to a grand jury in Washington, DC.

Dr Melkonian said the findings could lead Congress to determine Mr Musk as unfit for further dealings with the government.

"They could say, 'We're not going to authorise any more spending [on government contracts with Musk]'. That's their ultimate power. Congress controls the dollars," he said.

"Whether or not it ever goes to a federal judge, I don't think he likes that."

title: Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' as rain tumbles down
text:
Cattle prices jumped this week as heavy rain fell across key production areas in Queensland and northern New South Wales.

Meat and Livestock Australia's (MLA) benchmark Eastern Young Cattle Indicator (EYCI) surged beyond 1,000 cents a kilogram, as restockers and backgrounders competed for numbers.

"The cattle market shifted to a new gear off the back of this rain," Stuart Bull, MLA's market information manager said.

" Some of these regions were in need of a good drink and this rain has really helped pushed prices, along with fewer cattle coming to market. "

Demand for younger cattle was strong this week and the processor cow indicator hit a record high. (ABC Landline)

At Roma on Tuesday, some weaner steers from the Winton region sold for an incredible $7 a kilogram, which equated to more than $1,900 a head.

At Dubbo, the local saleyard report said restocker demand "sparked a market boom".

"Restocker demand was a stand-out, with young cattle selling up to an impressive 80 cents per kilo dearer [than last week]," the report said.

"Young steers reached a top of $7.40/kg, while young restocker heifers sold to $6.50/kg, showcasing the strength of competition and confidence among buyers looking to replenish their herds."

Loading...

Scott Loughnan, who runs a mixed farming operation west of Roma, had received more than 160 millimetres of rain when he spoke to ABC News.

"We'd organised to feed cattle all summer with forecasts of a super El Niño," he said.

"It was apparently never going to rain again, but this will definitely make it easier."

Mr Loughnan was in the middle of harvesting wheat, barley and chickpeas, and said for winter crops in the area, the rain was "not very good".

"I looked at some chickpeas this morning and they might not be much good, but I'm trying to look at the positives that this rain will grow us some grass and give us moisture for the next planting."

The MLA national indicators for processor cows and heavy steers have both reached record highs this week. (ABC Landline)

Record cow and heavy steers

Meanwhile, MLA's national processor cow indicator has cracked $4 a kilogram for the first time on record, and the national heavy steer indicator has also reached a new high of $4.77 a kilogram.

Global AgriTrends livestock analyst Simon Quilty said the supply of heavy steers was tight and processors were competing against feedlots to secure numbers.

"Once upon a time, feedlot operators wanted 450 kilogram to 500 kilogram steers, that was the preferred weight," he said.

"But that's now been lifted because of the lack of supply and they're taking 550 kilograms to almost 630 kilograms, creating an overlap [in demand] between processors and their needs for slaughter-ready cattle and the feedlotters who have extended the requirements of their cattle.

" So there's competition for numbers between the north and the south of Australia, plus processors versus feedlots [and] the net effect is this incredible demand for heavy steers that I think will continue. "

Mr Quilty believes Australia's cattle industry is at the start of a herd rebuild and is forecasting cattle prices to increase next year.

He is forecasting heavy steer prices to rise by about 20 per cent to about $5.70/kg next year.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview.

title: Can you stir-fry without gas? Fremantle pop-up serves up the answer
text:
An advocacy group for electric home conversion has set up a free noodle bar in Fremantle, WA to prove that giving up gas does not mean giving up your wok.

Electrify Fremantle's Wilf Johnston is one of the organisers of the Electric Noodle Bar and said the event, which is running as part of Fremantle Design Week, was about showing, rather than telling, people how living without gas could work.

"I think sometimes people need to tangibly see something, not just read about it on social media or online or a brochure," he said.

"Actually seeing something happening, and in this case smelling and tasting, really brings it home that it's possible to do this stuff."

Wilf Johnston chats to a customer while Amanda Auwdina stir-fires at the electric noodle bar event in Fremantle. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Feeling the heat of induction

Electrify Fremantle is a volunteer group that encourages and supports households to convert all their appliances to run on electricity so they can be powered by renewable energy.

Mr Johnston said for many people weighing up getting rid of their gas connection, cooking seemed to represent a particular quandary.

The electric noodle bar, where chef Amanda Auwdina whips up boxes of vegetarian noodles, aims to demonstrate that switching to an induction cooktop does not mean losing access to fast, intense heat.

A wok induction hotplate contains a dip for the wok to fit into. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

"We've got a flat-bottomed wok on a normal induction hot plate, which is great for everyday use," Mr Johnston said.

"We also have a curved induction wok burner, which is fantastic, which you use with a round wok, and the temperatures there you can get up to are easily adequate to get that nice wok flavour."

He said his research showed 40 per cent of households in Hong Kong now cooked with induction stoves, and they were becoming increasingly popular with businesses as well.

Plugging into curious shoppers

Having lured the electric-curious in with food, the group is also hoping to spark broader conversations about giving up gas.

"Normally when you talk about home electrification, you tend to get the people that are already on the journey and have already thought about it a lot, and that's great," Mr Johnston said.

"But for everyone else who might not be thinking about this, that's been our real target.

"People who are just walking through Fremantle on their way to do their shopping and have a coffee and whatever and had never really thought about this stuff are wandering in and having a chat, which is great."

While the organisers said there were range of arguments in favour of giving up gas stoves, from environmental benefits to easier cleaning, there was also a simpler rationale — it saves money, starting with the hundred of dollars a year it costs just to have a gas connection in Perth.

Research by consumer organisation Choice also found that induction cooktops transferred energy into cookware with about 85 per cent efficiency, compared to gas-powered cooking elements which operated at 32 per cent efficiency.

The Choice research found that induction cooktops were cheaper to run.

Research has found that induction cooking is more efficient than using gas. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Mr Johnston believed full electrification of homes across Perth was inevitable, and that gas would one day be phased out, which will happen in Albany over the next three years.

"I think it's interesting because the [Perth] gas network is not owned by the government, it's owned by a private company," he said.

"What we saw in Albany is that it just wasn't viable anymore, and I think over time, logically, you have to think that that is likely to be the case across the board.

"Nothing stops people using bottled gas, if that's really something that people want to keep doing.

"But I think the viability of the gas network will be called into question in the coming years for sure."

title: Former AFLW coach says likely player exodus to go 'well beyond Collingwood'
text:
Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.

The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.

"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.

"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."

Sam Wright took over as head coach at the end of 2023 and has struggled to get wins on the board since. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.

"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.

"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.

"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."

Ruby Schleicher, captain of Collingwood, will leave the Magpies at the end of the AFLW season. (Getty: Martin Keep)

Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.

Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.

He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.

Former player and coach Lauren Arnell slams non-offensive styles of play in the AFLW. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.

"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.

"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."

Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.

Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.

Essendon players have looked frustrated and dejected after losses this season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.

There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.

On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.

"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

title: 'Esther you can do that': Perth woman, 75, smashes handstand record
text:
Perth woman Esther Fischer has turned the record books upside down, becoming the world's oldest person to perform a handstand.

To break the world record, the 75-year-old retiree had to hold the stance for at least 15 seconds with no assistance.

To break the record, Esther Fischer needed to hold the stance for at least 15 seconds with no assistance. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

On August 31, she did not just break the record - she smashed it.

"I did 55 seconds, not just 15," she said.

"If you Google me, who's the oldest person who can hold a handstand, my name comes up.

" It's kind of cool. "

Ms Fischer said the idea was struck over a coffee with friends, after someone questioned who might have held such a record.

Their research told them it was a 74-year-old man from the United States.

"The girls said to me, 'Esther, you can do that,'" Ms Fischer said.

Esther Fischer took up her fitness journey later in life. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"And I looked at his handstands online on the Guinness Book of Records, and I thought, yeah, I can do that, I think."

Ms Fischer said that while she could already do a handstand, it was not something she mastered overnight.

"It took me three years," she said.

"It just took ages and ages and ages and one day I hit it.

"It was unreal."

Esther Fischer says her next challenge is to do a one-arm handstand. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Her accomplishment has inspired others to take on the challenge.

The gym where Ms Fischer has been a member for 10 years introduced a longevity class.

Gym owner Jacob Moffitt said the class is about helping people 60 and over get strong.

"[It improves] their quality of movement and their quality of life," he said.

Esther Fischer completed the feat in August but was only certified this week. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"Esther's one of the primary students of that class as well, and that's now attracted probably half a dozen [people] that come along to that class regularly."

Mr Moffitt said Ms Fischer is a good example that people can start at any time.

"She was never a gymnast, was never an athlete in her youth, she just started at 65 years old or 64, I think and then went from there," he said.

Ms Fischer said she is proud of her accomplishment but is already setting her mind to a new goal.

"I'm working on a one-arm [handstand]," she said.

Jacob Moffitt says Esther Fisher is a great example that exercise can start at any age. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"I've been doing that for two years now, and it's very hard.

"I could be the oldest person to do it, but I don't know whether it's going to work or not."

title: Aussie Picklum aglow on top of WSL standings after Portugal win
text:
Molly Picklum has hit peak form riding the celebrated Supertubos waves to win the Rip Curl Pro Portugal event and move back to pole position to retain her world surfing title.

"Right now I'm on top of the world … literally!" roared the 23-year-old Australian after her victory over America's former world champion Caitlin Simmers in Friday's final sent her back to the top of the World Surf League standings.

Picklum's triumph at one of surfing's most famous venues gave her the maximum 10,000-point haul to ensure she overhauled Hawaiian Carissa Moore at the top.

The win came at the perfect post-season moment with just two events left.

The Gosford star has enjoyed a shiny nickname since she referred to herself as like "a glow worm in a cave" riding inside a deep barrel wave.

So she was quick to offer a shout-out to her friends and family at home, whom she knew would be watching her first triumph of the season in the early hours.

"I just want to say thank you to all of them. I know they stayed up for this one. The glow worm absolutely did it and I love you all so much!" Picklum said.

The Australian was given a triumphant ride on a jet ski after clinching the final win before she threw herself into the water to celebrate.

"I just love it when I get to win in front of them and actually do it for them," she said.

"So many people support me and put so much energy into me. I just love winning to give back to those ones that give to me.

"I wanted to do well here. It was a dream of mine for me. Supertubos, it's like a cross between the Brazil energy and then (Hawaiian) Pipeline and those two together are like my two favourite things.

"So, oh my God, I'm so so grateful to win here. It was literally a dream of mine, and dreams come true. It's so baffling."

Picklum was delighted to "kind of hit my stride right at the right time" as she now sits atop the leaderboard on 48,950 points to Moore's 47,065, with another Hawaiian, Gabriela Bryan, third on 44,865 with two events left, the Philippines Pro and Pipeline.

Picklum didn't have a great record against 2024 world champ Simmers, having lost six of their previous eight head-to-head contests, but she was in control of the final from the moment she delivered a superb 7.83-point effort on her third wave to build on her opening 5.50.

Simmers couldn't respond, offering Picklum's fans on the beach a belated scare when she managed a best of 6.67 on the ninth of her 11 rides, but the Australian, who only had a half-dozen rides, eventually triumphed with her combined two-wave score of 13.33 to the American's 12.84.

title: Education support limit frustrates parents with type 1 diabetic children
text:
Every day and every night, Alana Marshall is monitoring her son's type 1 diabetes.

"When you have a child with type 1, it's a financial cost, it impacts your employment, you have this mental load, day and night, you lose sleep a lot of times," she said.

For the beginning of her son Declan's schooling in Capel, about 200 kilometres south of Perth, he has received extra support in the classroom.

In WA, individual disability allocation funding for children with type 1 diabetes is provided until the end of year two.

Declan was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at five years old. (Supplied: Alana Marshall)

Ms Marshall said it was frustrating to be told her son would have to manage his condition on his own at the age of eight.

Schools can apply for funding extensions, which consider medical evidence and circumstances on a case-by-case basis.

Policy 'unfair'

Ms Marshall said extra support for Declan was approved for year three, but the school would need to apply for the funding each year for ongoing support.

She said the policy was unfair for families already under pressure.

Alana Marshall says Declan's diabetes requires constant vigilance at school, including monitoring blood glucose levels and insulin. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

"He [Declan] has an implant in his arm … that takes a blood sugar reading every five minutes and sends that data to his phone," she said.

"My husband and I wear watches and the teacher has a watch which shows his levels because his blood sugar can drop really quickly if he's exercising, if he's playing soccer or something.

"If his blood sugar gets too low, that's when he can become unconscious, have a seizure and without intervention, that can be fatal.

"To have this on top of … OK, well now your child's turned eight so each year we need you to justify why he should get support, when it's a lifelong chronic health condition that adults struggle to manage, it felt really frustrating."

Support funding can be used by schools for an education assistant to help staff classrooms and with diabetes management.

A petition for change

Ms Marshall created a petition that will go to WA parliament, calling for the removal of the year two cut-off and extension of funding until the end of primary school.

The petition has attracted more than 800 signatures.

WA Shadow Education Minister Liam Staltari, who is facilitating Ms Marshall's petition, said the policy was outdated.

"The truth is with modern devices, these kids absolutely need the help," he said.

"What we can't have is kids being forced to manage a potentially life-threatening condition on their own, in busy, complex classrooms."

Perth Children's Hospital diabetes clinical lead Dr Craig Taplin said managing type 1 diabetes had significantly changed with advances in technology, including insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitoring.

He said families and children living with type 1 made hundreds of decisions a day, including calculating nutrients, carbohydrates and administering insulin.

Craig Taplin says the management of diabetes has changed significantly. (Supplied: Kids Research Institute Australia)

"It really is a 24/7 condition for children, adolescents and their parents and caregivers who are taking on a lot of that cognitive burden or cognitive load," he said.

"We do know that pumps and continuous glucose monitoring takes a significant proportion of that cognitive burden and offloads it some degree to an automated system.

"But there are still many, many interactions and points during a normal day in a healthy, active child where they still require thought and interaction."

Mr Taplin said there were about 1,300 children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes in WA, with three to four new children or adolescents diagnosed every week on average.

Review of policy in 'near future'

WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said support funding could be extended beyond year two.

"With each application on a case to case basis, considering the student's circumstances and supporting medical evidence," she said.

"I have asked the Department of Education to provide me with further advice on what the extension process involves, and how schools support families throughout this process."

Sabine Winton says funding could be extended on a case-by-case basis. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Ms Winton said students' health care needs were managed in accordance with a departmental policy that was due for review in the "near future".

title: NSW rail timetable changes axed after backlash from commuters
text:
Major changes to train timetables in Sydney and the Illawarra have been scrapped less than a month before they were due to begin after a backlash from commuters.

The state government last week announced more frequent services along the T4, T8 and South Coast lines, but some trips were expected to take longer.

In a backflip, Premier Chris Minns on Saturday said the changes due to take effect on November 15 would no longer go ahead after it had become clear "the vast majority of people do not want this new timetable".

"The truth of the matter is, since we released the train timetable I haven't run into anybody who supported the change," Mr Minns said.

He apologised to commuters for "putting them out".

"I'd rather apologise and backflip on a policy like this than implement a change that people don't want.

"I want the public to know that they've got a government that will listen to them, and also say when we get it wrong, 'We get it wrong'."

Chris Minns says the government has listened to commuters. (ABC News)

The proposed timetable was designed to deliver more frequent services and additional capacity across southern Sydney and the South Coast.

Transport Minister John Graham last week described the reliability of the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line as a "real issue".

He said the timetable changes and the addition of 200 more services a week would deliver shorter wait times.

Frequency on the T4 was expected to increase from a train every 10 minutes to one every 7.5 minutes during peak times.

The proposed changes raised concerns from passengers and MPs.

Commuters have opposed the timetable changes. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Mr Minns confirmed the existing timetable would remain in place and acknowledged that reliability on the network was a primacy concern for commuters opposing the changes.

"I want to make it clear that we will not be pursuing timetable changes unless, and until, reliability returns particularly to the T4 transport line," he said.

"There are still too many signal failures, breaks in the rail and major disruptions and we need to make sure that that is a reliable public transport option … and right now, to be perfectly candid with you, that is not the case."

After feedback from the community and MPs, Mr Graham said, the government was firmly focused on "reliability first" and that some progress had been made, but there was more to do.

Sydney Airport sore point

One sore point was fewer direct trips to Sydney Airport for passengers travelling from Wollongong because of the planned bypass of Wolli Creek.

The loss of the stop would mean changing at Sutherland or Hurstville, then again at Wolli Creek, or travelling into Central and catching an airport train back south.

A key part of the plan was the untangling of the Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra Line, and the South Coast Line to reduce bottlenecks and improve reliability.

The lines currently share a stretch of track, meaning a problem at Bondi Junction can cause delays on the South Coast.

The T8 would not longer have stopped at Sydenham, meaning an extra change to get on the Metro for travellers coming from south-western suburbs.

They would also have lost direct access to St Peters, Erskineville and Redfern stations at peak times.

The Member for Oatley, Mark Coure, released a political attack add against the changes. (Supplied)

The lines run through the electorate of Oatley, which Labor is hoping to seize from Liberal Mark Coure, who holds it by a wafer margin of 0.8 per cent.

Mr Coure seized on the changes in an attack ad that claimed Labor was delivering slower trips and creating an extra delay of 14 minutes.

"The public anger and pressure has been huge on Labor," Mr Coure told the ABC.

"This is a political backflip that would not have happened if the community had not called it out."

title: Nearly 30-year-old Magnum ice cream found in shop freezer
text:
The original Magnum Ego has been a quintessential ice cream in Australian households for decades — a perfect summer's day snack for millions across the country.



The much-loved ice cream was introduced in 1998, but was discontinued earlier this year, to the surprise of many.



However, earlier this week, a regional Victorian shop owner struck gold, accidentally stumbling upon an almost 30-year-old Magnum Ego tucked away in the back of his freezer.

Ash Standbridge, the owner of the Kolmar House General Store in Harrow, in Victoria's south-west, discovered the original Magnum Ego from the late '90s.

"At first I was a bit amazed and in a bit of disbelief," he said.

"I was just routinely clearing out a freezer and, as you do, you're chipping away at it and the ice and there was something underneath that I saw and noticed the old logo and the old wrapper and I'm like, 'Well, that's been here a while.'

" And, amazingly, it was still solid and intact; so frozen in time. "

Ash Standbridge says he is amazed he found the decades-old ice cream in his freezer. (Supplied: Ash Standbridge)

The general store has more than 145 years of history but Mr Standbridge took over the business just 10 months ago.

The famed freezer treat he discovered was a big favourite with ice cream lovers, consisting of a stick of vanilla ice cream covered in a thin milk chocolate layer, then a caramel layer and then an outer shell of milk chocolate.

"I was a kid in the late '90s and I remember it being a pretty big deal at the time. It was that sort of top-tier ultimate ice cream that people went crazy for," he said.

"So, as soon as I saw that wrapper, those sorts of memories came flooding back.

"I remember Friday night ice-cream runs to the servo with the family, and we were definitely a Magnum family. I remember the Ego just being that top-tier supreme one."



Mr Standbridge took to social media to post the discovery, which went viral, but unlike some courageous individuals in the comments, he said he wasn't brave enough to eat it.



"I ate two a day for a week when they came out," one commented on a Reddit feed.



While another said they "still look for them, and they've been gone for so long", while others recalled walking their "dog 10 times for one Magnum Ego".

Harrow's Kolmar House is more than 145 years old. (Supplied: Facebook)

Mr Standbridge had contacted the Magnum Ice Cream company about his find, and it is looking into it.

"Australians have been sharing stories, memories and tributes to Magnum Ego, reminding us just how special the product remains to so many people," the company said.

"We've loved seeing the conversation unfold and hearing people's memories of one of Australia's most iconic ice creams.



"For now, all we can say is watch this space."

More historic items found

The finds did not stop with the ice cream. Mr Standbridge managed to uncover multiple souvenirs from over the decades, in the same storeroom the freezer was in.

"I found old chip packets, again from the '80s and '90s," he said.

"I found a flavoured milk that was still sealed, but with no liquid on the inside, so the liquid had disappeared."



Mr Standbridge was in no rush to throw them away, keeping many of the items, which were all part of his store's unique history.

title: Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
text:
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.

The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.

'You can't be what you can't see' As she prepares for her final Test appearance, Emily Chancellor reflects on the legacy she leaves in Australian women's rugby.

But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.

"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.

"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].

"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.

"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.

"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.

Piper Duck scored one of the Wallaroos' five tries in their 38-31 win over Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.

The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.

But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

title: Darwin home owners selling up in nation's 'strongest property market'
text:
Lisa-Joy Cron bought her Palmerston home in 2010, just before Darwin's property market crashed — now, with prices rising after more than a decade of stagnation, she's weighing up selling before a possible downturn.

"I think right now is a good time to sell," she said.

"Purely because of the profit I could potentially make, and to take advantage of the good market in the Northern Territory at the moment … particularly with the interest rate rises."

Ms Cron said if she were to sell right now, she hoped her property would go for at least $300,000 more than what she bought it for 16 years ago.

Why housing is the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds.

A growing number of Darwin home owners and investors are listing their properties to cash in on rising prices, but experts at real estate analytics company Cotality warn there may only be a small window to get a good price.

Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said Darwin was defying the national property price slump, recording the "strongest property market in the country".

Property prices increased only modestly for the month of September, with house prices up 0.3 per cent and units up 0.8 per cent.

He said Darwin was now the only capital city where house prices were rising, largely due to limited supply and years of sluggish building activity.

Although more home owners were listing their properties, Mr Burg said there were fewer buyers, indicating the tight property market may be gradually unwinding.

Property prices are continuing to rise in Darwin. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"There is still some uncertainty around where property demand is heading in the coming months," he said.

"There is the risk, of course, that the RBA may do another hike to the interest rates in November, and that would have another further impact.

" So it is possible that Darwin might start to experience the broader national downturn that we're seeing. "

He said the market was already showing signs of cooling.

"At the midpoint of January, [the total number of properties for sale was] around 60 per cent below average," Mr Burg said.

"It's now sitting around 40 per cent below average and is continuing to track up."

Real estate agent Kerri-Ann Laurence, who has sold homes across Darwin for more than two decades, has also noticed an uptick in listings since January but said "historically, it's still quite low".

She said the majority of her clients were either relocating, moving for family reasons, upsizing or downsizing.

Kerri-Ann Laurence has worked in Darwin for more than two decades. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I've no doubts some of the downsizers in particular are seizing the opportunity," she said.

Ms Laurence said she'd also noticed the recent wave of interstate investors — who, over the past year, had been snapping up properties across greater Darwin within days of them being listed — was now easing as prices continued to rise.

However, she said she expected the market to remain on an upward trajectory.

"There's been plenty of projects on the boil — Beetaloo gas is now flowing, I think that will lead to more investment, and in a small town like Darwin, it doesn't take much," she said.

" If one of these projects needs 1,000 [workers] on the ground, that's going to make a dramatic difference in the real estate landscape overnight. "

Darwin remains among the most expensive capital cities to rent a home, ranking third behind Sydney and Perth.

Cost-of-living pressure 'entrenching disadvantage' in the NT The NT has some of the country's most expensive rental costs, with households having to set aside more of their weekly wages to cover the price of essentials.

Cotality's latest data revealed the median dwelling rental cost rose by about 11.6 per cent year on year, as of September.

The Top End city's vacancy rate remained tight, sitting at about 1.9 per cent, Mr Burg said.

"That means that in some locations in Darwin, it is actually cheaper to purchase the house under a mortgage than it is to rent a similar property," he said.

The shortfall in new home construction paints a bleaker picture for renters outside the capital, with the vacancy rate in Alice Springs sitting at just 1.4 per cent.

title: Vintage car rally celebrates the Ford Model A
text:
Dozens of vintage cars have descended on Western Australia's far south coast in the country's largest gathering of Ford Model As.

It was a rare glimpse into the past for the early colonial town of Albany, 400 kilometres south of Perth, with the sounds of vintage car horns flooding its historic precinct on Friday.

Model As line up in Albany for the vintage car rally. (ABC News: Rachel Jennings)

Rally director Andrae Moore said some of the restored cars travelled from nearly every state in the country, while others came from further away.

"Then we've had participants actually join us without their cars from New Zealand, the United Kingdom and Slovenia," she said.

Andrae Moore says dozens of cars took part in the rally. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Century of preservation

Produced in the early 1900s, the Model A was one of the most well-known and top-selling cars in America.

"All the [second] Model As are from 1928 through to 1931 and came after the infamous Model T," Ms Moore said.

Ford Model A enthusiasts from across the globe travelled to Albany for the rally. (ABC News: Rachel Jennings)

" These cars were special because they were the everyman's car, and they were allowed to be in any colour — they didn't have to be black like the Model T. "

For many of the members, the cars are treasured possessions and owned to be driven.

Eighty-two-year-old Ben Munneke estimated he drove his Model A 5,000 kilometres from Maleny in Queensland to Albany for the rally.

"It was good fun driving, a lot of stops along the Nullarbor; there's not a lot of comfortable places to stay, but we made it, and we enjoyed doing it," he said.

Flags of origin on display

For Steve Watson and his friends, the travel was much further as they flew from Yorkshire in England and borrowed a car so they could take part in the event.

"We have borrowed a car, and we've adorned it with suitable patriotic flags so everybody knows where we've come from," he said.

Steve Watson travelled all the way from Yorkshire in the UK to join the rally. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Watson said there were similar clubs in the UK but not at the same level as the Australian meeting.

"There is a Model A club in England, and we have about 300 members, but the participation in an event like this is not as good," he said.

title: ‘Slow burn’: Western Sydney Airport’s real challenge awaits after launch
text:

As the new airport opens in western Sydney, we take a look at how it became a reality. See all stories .

Once Western Sydney International Airport opens on Sunday, the true strength of demand for flights from Australia’s newest airport will start to show. But success won’t happen overnight, aviation experts say. The curfew-free airport is expected to benefit from Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport’s limits on capacity. But its growth may be held back by passengers’ unwillingness to try the new hub some 50 kilometres away from Sydney’s CBD, as well as airlines’ reluctance to fly there. How busy will it get? An artist’s render of Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport. Australia’s first newly built airport in more than half a century is launching at a time of spiralling costs for airlines amid surging fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East, and the kind of global uncertainty that makes market predictions difficult. But playing in its favour are Sydney Airport’s well-known issues with capacity, which are often worsened by its air traffic control staffing issues, inclement coastal weather conditions and a strict curfew, which prevents night take-offs and landings.

Advertisement

With those conflicting factors, it’s perhaps not surprising that only seven airlines have committed to fly out of WSI so far, averaging about six return flights a day, domestic and international routes combined. Sydney Airport, by contrast, is at near capacity with about 400 return flights a day across almost 60 airlines. ‘Many big cities globally have two or more commercial airports. It was absolutely necessary here as well.’ Former IATA business strategist Tony Laverghetta Qatar Airways finally committed to flying to WSI this week, though not before late 2027. With crude oil at more than $US100 a barrel, airlines can’t afford to fly uneconomical routes. High costs and a shortfall of new airframes have limited the availability of planes and pilots. Perhaps for this reason, Qantas will run only four return flights per week to Brisbane and four flights per week to Melbourne when it starts to fly from WSI on March 28, 2027, using 95-seat QantasLink Embraer E190 aircraft. Air New Zealand will fly three times weekly to WSI from Auckland.

Advertisement

After that, it depends on how well things go. Senior aviation consultant Ian Guy says that if airlines make more money off their routes at WSI than elsewhere, they’ll stick with it. But if the routes are unprofitable, after a season or a couple of years they’ll to pull the flights. ‘Slow burn’ A look overseas offers examples of the dynamics starting to play out at WSI. Secondary airports operating far from the city centres they nominally serve, tend to attract low-cost airlines that effectively “plant a flag” to watch the demand, says Guy, who is a director at Melbourne-based Tango 5 aviation consultancy. A carrier can then quickly scale up if demand supports it. Qantas-owned Jetstar has made the biggest commitment to WSI so far. Jetstar will fly up to 24 return services a week from Western Sydney, with up to 14 to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast, and three a week to Brisbane.

Advertisement

Vietnam-based low-cost carrier Vietjet will start flying two return services a week to Ho Chi Minh City in January. The airline’s stablemate Vietjet Thailand is expected to begin flying four times a week to Bangkok in November 2027. In addition to Air New Zealand’s commitment, Singapore Airlines will have one daily return flight from WSI to Singapore Changi. Related Article Aviation 80 years in the making: How Sydney’s new international airport finally took off Behind the scenes, subsidies for operational fees are also a factor. A $16 million Western Sydney International Take-Off Fund backed jointly by the airport and the NSW state government has been designed to help woo airlines to the new airport. Yet what happens after the initial sweetener is a different matter, Guy says, and it’s possible that “once that subsidy falls away, the route doesn’t have the same economics and so it stops existing.”

Advertisement

Ellis Taylor, Asia editor for aviation analytics company Cirium, expects the new airport uptake would be “a bit of a slower burn” but WSI’s ability to operate late at night and early in the morning adds “an interesting dynamic”. ‘More than just the poor man’s Sydney Airport’ WSI is “more than just the poor man’s Sydney Airport,” Taylor says, comparing its premise with when Jetstar began flying from Avalon in 2004. “It’s not really sort of seen as an alternative to the main airport as yet. It’s more about opening up an additional demand point,” she says. And once that is done, the airport’s viability in the larger aviation market will be tested. Yet, in other ways, WSI and Avalon could not be more different. While WSI is built on the expectation of expanding commercial flights to Sydney’s west, Avalon was built in the 1950s for use by military planes and only turned into a commercial airport in the 1990s. A view from the new airport’s top floor, where international passengers will arrive. Sitthixay Ditthavong

Advertisement

Melbourne Tullamarine, Victoria’s primary airport, has plenty of capacity, hosts more than 40 airlines (including, from this month, Finnair) and operates without a curfew. Avalon is operating against an unconstrained competitor. In turn, it has sought to specialise and tap the growing logistics and freight sectors to link Victoria to export markets in the Middle East. The proximity of airports often shape where airlines base themselves. In London, Heathrow is the premium airport, serving alongside smaller airports Gatwick, Stansted and Luton, which function as hubs for low-cost carriers such as easyJet, Ryanair, and Wizz Air. Related Article Aviation Qatar Airways plans flights to western Sydney from late 2027 “If you really looked at the density of their flight operations...they have each picked particular airports to focus on,” says Guy. A UK-based network planner with knowledge of the Australian market believes WSI will be a success, as it adds real international capacity to the city.

Advertisement

“It relieves Sydney’s peak-slot scarcity and it’s curfew-free, so carriers can build in the late-night and early morning departures that make European connections work” – a big advantage over Kingsford Smith, she points out. Western Sydney is also “a big, multicultural catchment with strong VFR [visiting friends and relatives] demand and family ties abroad”.WSI will target the leisure and visiting friends and relatives market, which is cheaper, volume-led, she says, “while Kingsford Smith holds the premium end”. The VFR market has its own dynamic. People typically take fewer trips, but travel in bigger groups. They tend to fly on less expensive fares, too, and have more luggage. This could be a positive for WSI’s launch, as passengers are likely to travel by car and won’t be dissuaded by WSI’s nascent ground transportation. Escalators and stairs link a bag-drop area to departures on the first level. Sitthixay Ditthavong VFR represents a significant plank of the aviation market in Australia. NSW Premier Chris Minns has been courting India as a major source of visitors to the state. But demographics don’t mean an automatic embrace from homeland airlines.

Advertisement

In a media presentation early this month by Air India head of global sales Manish Puri played down the possibility of serving WSI for now, saying that while the “options of opening new stations always remain… initially, our intention is to densify our current network” with more frequencies. About 60 per cent of Air India traffic to and from Australia is VFR, Puri says, and while VFR will remain a “strong point” for the airline, Air India wants to move more into meeting demand for travel to Europe. The addition of WSI to Australia’s network of airports could spur other changes too. Loading Perth-based senior aviation consultant Bill Meeke says the combination of the curfew at Sydney Airport and the three-hour time zone difference with Western Australia during daylight saving means that “the daily window of access for flights from Perth is very narrow for much of the year”. Curfew-free flights at WSI could change that.

Advertisement

As the new airport finds its place in the national aviation grid, it may spur other opportunities. It’s possible an overseas carrier would make WSI a stopover between a domestic airport and an international destination to pick up enough passengers to make its flight profitable. There could be a route like Cairns-Western Sydney-Hong Kong, for example, where passengers from two domestic points are used to fill the plane. Related Article Aviation How chook farm spurred Paul Keating’s push for new airport at Badgerys Creek Once WSI kicks into gear and proves a business success for the first airlines, it could become a meaningful competitor to Sydney Airport and force the city’s long-established hub to lift its game, says Guy. Unable to add a lot more airlines, Sydney Airport will then have to help carriers up-gauge their aircraft, accommodating larger-capacity, bigger planes, he says. But that’s in the future. “I suspect at the moment they’re not overly worried.”

Tony Laverghetta, a former International Air Transport Association business strategist, says it will take time, but eventually WSI “will become a solid option for travellers”, especially when its new metro line opens. “Many big cities globally have two or more commercial airports,” Laverghetta says, pointing to London, New York, Milan and Paris. “It was absolutely necessary here as well.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Sitthixay Ditthavong Preliminary figures show 20,000 endoscopy procedures could be overdue, with final figures still to be validated. Waiting times for endoscopies have been a long-standing challenge for the health system because of the growing demand, an ageing population and increasing referrals through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program. The government will spend $17 million boosting endoscopy capacity beginning with the most urgent cases. title: This genre-bending novel blends mystery, romance and art history
text:
Gates’ fiction is often hilarious and tongue-in-cheek, especially when he relays his unreliable narrator’s penchant for mansplaining thesis ideas to anyone who will (or won’t) listen, including bartenders and sunbaking Dutch tourists. The reader can occasionally feel like someone trapped on an aeroplane next to a passenger who won’t stop talking. Gates is well aware of this, though, and introduces a wonderful parallel narrative where Tiffen falls in love with Agnés, who he meets staring at a painting in a Sydney art gallery. From Barcelona, she works at the Berowra Waters Inn, and Tiffen encircles her in a bid to win her affections; he desperately needs a muse.

Playing detective is Christopher Tiffen, a PhD student writing an art history thesis and scrambling for clues on what happened to Wake: Did he go to prison during the Spanish Civil War? Where have his artworks gone? Is he still alive? Any PhD student in writing and literature or art history researcher will get a kick out of Gates’ blurring of genres and Tiffen’s hapless and fantasist attempts to fit his findings into academic parameters when he really wants to explode the narrative. Art lovers will see pointers everywhere to artworks and painters, as Tiffen recognises the brushstrokes of places he visits.

Roaming between Sydney and Hydra, Hill End and Barcelona, London and Paris, Geoffrey Gates’ third novel, The Phantom Surrealist , is a playful search for an elusive Australian artist, Robert J Wake, who grows up on the gritty streets of Surry Hills and ends up on surrealist shores with Miro and Picasso. Soon after, he disappears in Spain.

This contemporary narrative cleverly echoes Wake’s journey: Wake sailed to pre-World War II London while Tiffen flies into Heathrow; Tiffen works alone in a Kombi Van in Hill End, where Wake painted in an abandoned cottage. Eventually, the narratives have to intersect, and they do in a deus ex machina that seems too insanely neat, but perhaps not for the imaginings of Tiffen; he is searching for “the uncomfortable depths where the fluid truth lies”, after all.

Gates’ central exploration is of fantasy and escape, fakery and the false motivations we project onto others – who we know and who we imagine we know – the stories we make to fill in the gaps when there are no answers. Tiffen is like a phantom in his own life, too, curiously lacking self-awareness. At times the interplay between the parallel narratives seems too delineated. Perhaps more blurring of lines between character, time and space would have kept it aptly surreal and uncertain.

Ultimately, the book is an examination of what tends to fall through the cracks. The painters’ women-lovers who meld into the muse landscape rather than being recognised for their own work and activism. The pre/postwar Australian artists who leave our shores to become key figures in international art scenes but don’t exist in the galleries, catalogues and archives. It’s no surprise that Wake works in the propaganda unit in Spain and the camouflage unit in Australia – where his work is transitory and has no signature. Even Hill End, once thriving but now abandoned, has become the “land of disappearance”.

The Phantom Surrealist is an enticing novel that dissects the narrative of what it means to be an Australian artist like Robert J Wake in the world, and what it takes to find a sense of home. Caught in the tension between knowing everything about art, and not able to express himself as an artist, Tiffen has to make do with losing himself in the imagined lives of others. Gates threads these two characters’ worlds together skilfully, shaping a mysterious ficto-biography of artistic grandeur, that also manages to have a lot of fun along the way.

Cape Town: Travis Head has pushed back against calls to regenerate the Test team, arguing Australia should maintain their recent policy to reinforce a “strong team” with seasoned players from domestic ranks, and not radically alter things due to one “shithouse day” that cost them the second Test against South Africa. Following his rearguard century, featuring a long partnership with nightwatchman Scott Boland, Head admitted the team had identified an underperforming batting order as an issue to be addressed before this series, but could not put his finger on why they had not managed to pass 400 in an innings since January last year – 10 Test matches ago. But Head’s most striking message was that strong teams should be reinforced with senior players while weaker teams rebuild, adamant that Australia must be considered the former.

“The times that you’ve seen strong Australian cricket teams, you’ve seen older guys come in because I think just it’s a byproduct of how strong the Test team is,” Head said. “It’s great that we’ve got a strong Test team. I’m going to miss people, but guys that have played a lot of first-class cricket. Loading “Then you skip a generation, you go to Sam Konstas and the [Ollie] Peakes and the [Campbell] Kellaways. I have confidence in the next man in being an experienced 32-year-old like a Jake Weatherald or Pete Handscomb, Kurtis Patterson, who have all done well. “I think right now it’s that we’ve got a strong Australian cricket team. title: 'You'll never forget the very first flight': How a new airport became a bucket-list item
text:
John Darcy had never set foot on a plane until he was 40.

Now, 18 years and 179 flights later, he'll be on the first international flight to leave Western Sydney International Airport.

The Sydney aviation enthusiast spent his childhood photographing planes and dreaming of travelling on one. On Monday morning, he'll board Air New Zealand flight NZ166 to Auckland, becoming one of the first international passengers to depart from Australia's newest airport.

"I started keeping account of my flights; it's become a hobby, collecting airports, collecting flight routes, collecting different types of planes flown on," Darcy told SBS News.

"I've flown 179 times, more than 60 airports in Australia, North America and Europe.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"But I needed to add Western Sydney International Airport to my tally."

Darcy is old enough to remember when the Hawke government announced Badgerys Creek as the site for Sydney's second airport.

Dubai from the air during one of Darcy's 179 flights. Source: Supplied

After decades of debate, delay and construction, he said it felt only right to be there from the start.

"It's been so long coming. To think that on Sunday, passengers will start flying in and out of there, and on Monday I will be on the first international flight out of there."

"It's for the little boy inside of me."

Sydney's second airport will welcome its first passengers this weekend, becoming Australia's first newly built international airport in more than 50 years.

Located near Badgerys Creek in western Sydney, the airport will initially host services from airlines including Jetstar, Qantas, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet.

Unlike Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, flights can arrive and depart around the clock.

For aviation enthusiasts like Darcy, that makes the opening more than just an infrastructure project.

A few hours in Auckland

The destination, however, is almost beside the point.

Darcy will spend just one night in Auckland before flying home the following day.

"The only reason I'm doing this is for that inaugural flight," he said.

"I don't have any particular business in Auckland and I need to get back to resume work. I'm not taking holidays for this, just a couple of days off."

Four weeks later, he'll do something similar again, flying on Singapore Airlines' inaugural service from Western Sydney to Singapore.

"I'll be overnight in Auckland on Monday, but four weeks later when I go to Singapore, I'll be five hours in Changi Airport and then coming straight back."

"It's the novelty of the new airport and the badge of honour of being on the first international departure from that airport," he said.

There's also data behind that badge of honour.

Since 2014, he has logged every flight he can remember taking, tracking everything from flight numbers and aircraft types to which day of the week he travelled.

"It's on an Excel spreadsheet," he said.

"I've tracked all the data of the different flight sectors, the airlines, all the flight numbers, the length of all the flights, the departure airports, the arrival airports."

His trip from Western Sydney to Auckland has already been entered.

"It will be my 180th flight and 2,201 kilometres from Western Sydney to Auckland."

Darcy isn't the only aviation enthusiast making special plans for the airport's opening.

Some are buying tickets on inaugural flights. Others are heading to Sydney for a completely different view.

Chasing the perfect shot

For 19-year-old Alastair, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport is just as exciting. But while Darcy will be inside the plane, Alastair plans to be hundreds of metres away with a camera pointed at it.

The Melbourne plane spotter is flying to Sydney specifically to photograph the airport's first departures.

"I'm going up there to capture a moment in history because it's not every day that Australia gets a new international airport," he said. "It'll just be a once-in-a-lifetime thing."

Plane spotting, he explains, is about more than watching aircraft take off and land.

"It's like getting different plane liveries that normal people would see and think, 'Oh, that's just what a plane looks like'," he said.

"Sometimes there's a really special one, and it's very cool to see."

Plane spotter Alastair will be ready with a camera as the first flight takes off from Western Sydney International Airport. Source: Supplied

After discovering the hobby at 14, Alastair began keeping a notebook of every aircraft registration he spotted.

Five years on, that handwritten tally is closing in on 2,000 entries, and he now heads out plane spotting almost every day.

Sometimes that's at Melbourne Airport. Sometimes it's from a nearby park. Occasionally, it's from his own backyard.

What started with a phone camera has evolved into a serious setup worth about $5,000.

He uses flight-tracking apps to monitor aircraft movements and, when he's photographing at Melbourne Airport, often climbs ladders to shoot above the fence line.

Alastair uses ladders that can extend up to 6m to photograph planes above airport fence lines. Source: Supplied

"What we bring at Melbourne Airport are ladders," he said. "We bring ladders that can go three metres up so we can get a good shot above the fence line."

Fully extended, those ladders can reach 6m.

He's never fallen off one himself, although he's seen others take a tumble in pursuit of the perfect image.

The effort, he says, is worth it.

One of his favourite parts of the hobby is connecting with pilots, some of whom message him directly to ask for photos of their flights.

Pilots will sometimes acknowledge Alastair from the cockpit when he takes photos from the other side of the fence. Source: Supplied

"They'll wave from the cockpit or they'll do something to acknowledge me from the other side of the fence," he said.

"I think that's really cool."

A once-in-a-generation opening

Within Australia's plane spotting community, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport has become one of the most anticipated aviation events in years.

Alastair compares the excitement to the arrival of the Airbus A350-1000 ULR in Melbourne earlier this year, when aviation enthusiasts gathered to photograph the aircraft used during Qantas' record-breaking ultra-long-haul testing flights.

"I don't think anything will beat the hype of when the Airbus A350-1000 ULR came to Melbourne," he said.

"But the hype for Western Sydney, it's big.

"Everyone's excited to spot there. Everyone's excited to fly out of there. Everyone's excited to see what airlines will fly there."

Like Darcy, Alastair is interested in the history as much as the aircraft itself.

He's already hoping to capture a photo of the airport's first departures, particularly if one receives a ceremonial water-cannon salute.

But he says the real value of those images won't be obvious to everyone who sees them.

"It's like the backstory of the photos," he said.

"Someone's going to say, 'Oh, that's just a Jetstar plane taking off.'

"And I'd be like, 'No, that's the first passenger flight out of a new airport in so long in Australia.'

"You can always get a Jetstar A320 at Western Sydney in the next 20 years.

"But you'll never forget the very first flight."

title: Australians are having fewer babies. Can migration fill the gap?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

"I had my baby at 38," says Heer Kaur, an Indian migrant living in Beveridge, north of Melbourne, who had always imagined having a big family.

But the reality of building a life in a new country, establishing a career and raising a child without family support meant rethinking that dream.

Kaur eventually decided to have just one child, weighing her desire for a large family against the financial and practical demands of parenthood.

"As migrants, we have to rebuild everything in the new country. I kept postponing marriage or having children for later. I wanted to be settled first. Be a permanent resident, build a career, have some stability," she tells SBS Punjabi.

"I wanted to have at least two kids. I assumed I would be able to have kids whenever I tried. But that was not the case."
