SBS News has withheld her real name for privacy reasons.

Kaur says the lack of family support in Australia also meant spending more on childcare.

More money spent on childcare meant having to work longer to earn more, and then less time with my child. Then I had to settle for a quality life for my son, even though it meant him being an only child.

"The compromise comes with guilt as a parent. We work hard to ensure he learns social skills, how to share, and has a network of his own, beyond us."

She says she hopes the family she built was the result of her own choices, not dictated by social and economic circumstances.

Kaur's experience reflects a wider question facing Australia: what happens when the family people want, and the family they can afford, are not the same?

Previous Intergenerational Reports have predicted that Australia would have a higher fertility rate. Source: SBS News

Kaur is not alone in finding herself at this crossroads.

The Treasury's Intergenerational Report (IGR) 2026 puts Australia's total fertility rate at a historic low of 1.48 births per woman, lower than the total fertility rates projected in previous IGRs.

The replacement-level fertility rate — the rate at which a population replaces itself over time without migration — is about 2.1 births per woman.

The report projects that Australia's fertility rate will decline further to 1.34 births per woman by 2065–66.

It identifies delayed childbearing as a key factor contributing to smaller families and lower fertility rates.

Why are Australians delaying having kids?

The IGR identifies establishing a career as one reason people delay parenthood. It also points to access to childcare, the burden of unpaid care, housing security, and workplace flexibility as factors influencing people's decisions about whether to start a family or have more children.

The trend towards later childbearing is not unique to Australia.

In 2023, more than one in three births worldwide were to women aged 30 and over, compared with about one in four in 1990.

Source: SBS News

However, experts say delayed parenthood is only part of the picture. Financial pressures, changing social expectations and individual circumstances can also shape decisions about family size. The reasons vary, and lower fertility rates do not necessarily mean that everyone wants more children but is unable to have them.

But as Australia's fertility rate falls and its population ages, the implications extend beyond individual families.

The IGR warns that if birth rates and migration fall below baseline expectations, Australia's population would be 1.9 million smaller and the economy 7.4 per cent smaller by 2065–66.

And with deaths projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, migration is expected to play an increasingly important role in sustaining population growth and meeting workforce needs.

Australia's growing reliance on migration

Migrants already make up a large and growing share of the health care and social assistance workforce.

The IGR notes that migration can help moderate population ageing as new migrants are "typically younger than the existing population".

Source: SBS News

Demographer Liz Allen says Australia's ageing population and below-replacement fertility rate mean the country will rely more on migration to support its workforce and economy.

"Australia is on the way to what's considered super-aged. It essentially means that, in proportion speaking, we have more people aged over 65 than we have young people," she tells SBS Punjabi.

Demographer Liz Allen says Australia is moving towards becoming a super-aged society, meaning people aged 65 and over will make up a larger share of the population than younger Australians. Credit: Supplied

"Currently, we rely on individual income taxpayers to contribute to the economy; with an ageing population and below-replacement-level fertility, we have a shrinking relative working-age population. That means fewer tax dollars coming from that biggest source of taxpayers, individual workers."

At the moment, migrants present the biggest share of population growth in this country. And that's because the local population isn't growing the way it used to.

Allen says migration also brings social and cultural benefits alongside its economic contribution.

Source: SBS News

The IGR found new migrants are typically younger than the existing population, with a median age of 26 compared with 38 in 2024-25. As a result, migration helps slow population ageing and increases the share of working-age people beyond what would be achieved through natural increase alone.

Do migrants have more children?

Research by the University of Melbourne's demographer Peter McDonald shows that temporary migrants are predominantly young adults aged 20 to 35, many of whom come to Australia to study or establish their careers. While they are included in the population's childbearing age group, they contribute relatively few births.

Allen says migrants can also adopt the fertility patterns of their new country, which "in some cases, means even have lower fertility rates than the local population".

"Upon arrival in Australia, many migrants prioritise work and education, which delays family formation into their late 30s or beyond. This trend mirrors the broader patterns seen in the Australian population," she says.

Adelaide-based photographer Naina Redhu says the realities of parenthood are often underestimated. Credit: Supplied

For Adelaide-based freelance photographer Naina Redhu, moving to Australia meant meeting her partner, Jamie. While she says she is happy with her partner, neither of them wants to have children.

The 46-year-old says she has always been clear that she doesn't want children. Yet the decision has often prompted questions and unsolicited advice, including suggestions that she freeze her eggs as a precaution.

"My ex-husband and I were clear that we did not want children, but later, he did want to have kids some years down the line," she tells SBS Punjabi.

This is a fundamental choice; it narrates what kind of life you are choosing for yourself.

"I think it is selfish to have kids, and we ended up parting ways."

Redhu says not having a child doesn't mean she takes motherhood lightly.

"I believe parenting is a 24X7 commitment for the rest of your life. For someone like me, it would mean putting everything aside and being completely focused on raising the child, and I am not ready for that commitment yet," she says.

"There are so many things that I have to do and still want to do."

The barriers to having children

Allen says Australia should focus less on achieving an ideal number of children and more on removing hurdles that prevent people from having the families they want.

"We need to reach a point where having a much-wanted child, or a second child, is truly possible and not obstructed by barriers that feel insurmountable. Otherwise, the consequences ripple across society," she says.

She warns that smaller families may also have broader social consequences, including greater pressure on individuals to provide care for ageing relatives or fewer family connections to rely on.

Ultimately, having a child is not just a mother's responsibility; it is a societal concern.

"Until we address major challenges including housing affordability, economic security, climate change, and gender equality, Australians may lack the confidence and hope needed to plan for the future."

title: Caught out in a record-breaking storm: Why we didn't see it coming
text:
IN BRIEF: Rainfall and flash floods in south-east Queensland on Thursday far exceeded forecasts.

Experts say that while weather forecasting is always improving, climate change has complicated things.

A freak storm tore through south-east Queensland on Thursday, dumping more than 200mm of rain in three hours, leading to flash floods and hundreds of State Emergency Service calls.

Between Wednesday and Friday morning, at least eight weather stations just north of Brisbane in the catchments of the Pine and Caboolture rivers recorded huge 48-hour rainfall totals exceeding 300mm, according to weather tracking site Weatherzone.

While initial forecasts from the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) predicted that Thursday would be the wettest day of the week in parts of Queensland, the severity of the downpour was unprecedented. Monthly rainfall records were broken in Nambour on the Sunshine Coast, where a running total of 401mm to Friday morning broke the old October record of 370.6mm, and in Beerburrum, in the same region, where the running monthly total rainfall of 354.2mm broke the old October record of 311.5mm.

Earlier this week, the BoM was questioned over false rainfall predictions later revealed to be caused by Bogong Moth migration. There were other times when its forecasts were off track, including in August, when Queensland rain outpaced forecasts, and after the 2023-2024 summer, when the El Niño weather event the bureau had predicted failed to materialise.

Senior lecturer in climate science at the University of Melbourne, Andrew King, said that while weather forecasts have improved immensely over time, "that doesn't mean they're always perfect", especially when it comes to forecasting thunderstorms and rainfall.

"Small-scale storms, which can dump a lot of rainfall and have major impacts, are still hard to predict precisely, as it's difficult to forecast exactly where they'll occur, and that can mean forecast accuracy suffers, even over short timeframes."

READ MORE Wet weather expected to peak later in the week in soaked state

Smaller weather events like the thunderstorms in Queensland over the past few days are harder to represent in the models meteorologists use to simulate the atmosphere, he said.

Dr Michael Barnes from Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment told SBS News that while there had been vast improvements to the technology used to forecast weather, there were "limits to what is physically possible".

"Events such as thunderstorms that deliver 200 millimetres of rain within 24 hours are driven by highly localised atmospheric processes," he said.

"When weather is highly localised, even a small error can mean the storm's path or location isn't forecast particularly well.

"We often cannot know exactly where those storms will form or how intense they will become."

Weather forecasts are improving

"A seven-day forecast today is about as accurate as a two-day forecast was 40 years ago," Barnes said.

"There have been three major drivers of improved weather forecasting: better scientific understanding, greater computing power, and more observations.

"Twenty years ago, a forecast might have said that moderate rain was expected tomorrow afternoon. Today, people have weather apps that provide hourly rainfall forecasts and detailed estimates of expected precipitation."

READ MORE The El Niño backdrop that could spell trouble off Australia's coast

But he said that also meant expectations of weather forecasting have become much higher.

King agreed that there were higher expectations on the BoM, which he said had "certainly" come under scrutiny in recent years.

"Part of that is because Australians are relatively knowledgeable about climate drivers such as El Niño and La Niña. However, that understanding can sometimes become oversimplified."

But he warned that general understanding can sometimes "oversimplify" complex systems.

"People often hear 'El Niño' and assume conditions will be hot and dry. In reality, El Niño merely increases the likelihood of those outcomes; it doesn't guarantee them."

READ MORE El Niños could be more common in our future unless we change course, research suggests

Many factors influence Australia's weather, including the Indian Ocean, the Southern Ocean, Antarctica and tropical regions to the north.

"El Niño and La Niña are only part of the picture," he said.

"To be fair to the Bureau, it has tried to shift attention away from a narrow focus on those weather events and encourage people to pay more attention to seasonal outlooks, which incorporate all these influences."

SBS News has contacted the BoM for comment.

Climate change 'complicates' perceptions

When it comes to severe weather events, Barnes said, climate change "complicates things".

"Particularly in situations like the recent event in south-east Queensland, there is good evidence that daily and even sub-daily rainfall extremes are intensifying, primarily driven by thunderstorms," he said.

Produced by "the inherent chaos of the atmosphere", thunderstorms would continue to be challenging to predict.

While climate change doesn't necessarily reduce meteorologists' technical ability to forecast weather, it can affect how forecast accuracy is perceived.

Difficult-to-predict weather phenomena, such as localised severe thunderstorms, may be becoming "more consequential".

"As a result, it can appear that forecasts are becoming less reliable when, in reality, the impacts are increasing," Barnes said.

King from the University of Melbourne said climate scientists had discussed the tendency for "El Niño to become a scapegoat for everything that's happening in the climate system".

When people see severe weather during a strong El Niño, they naturally assume El Niño is the cause; however, climate change is operating in the background and is amplifying many extreme weather events.

"Climate change hasn't gone away. It's continuing to worsen as greenhouse gas emissions increase."

And climate change is "already" making extreme weather events worse, particularly heatwaves, which in Australia are more intense, more frequent and longer-lasting because of climate change.

But he said that as Australia's weather worsened, he understood the tendency to attribute severe weather to big events like El Niño and La Niña.

"There's a natural human desire to make sense of things that are difficult to understand," he said.

"Weather and climate are complicated, and reality is often more complex than it first appears."

title: Why millions of overseas basketball fans are following Sydney's newest star
text:
In Brief Chinese Olympian Yang Shuyu has brought millions of followers' attention to the WNBL.

Four Chinese national team players and a new broadcast deal are growing the league's reach in China.

A Chinese Olympian with more than five million online followers has made a winning start to life in Australia, helping the Sydney Flames to a dominant victory while drawing fresh attention to the Women's National Basketball League (WNBL) from fans across China.

Yang Shuyu scored 20 points in her first home game for the Flames on Saturday, helping guide the club to a 95-68 win over the Adelaide Lightning.

But the 24-year-old's arrival is about more than one player.

Yang — who has 5.3 million followers on Douyin, the Chinese equivalent of TikTok — is one of four Chinese national team stars in the league this season, as the WNBL looks to strengthen its presence in China and reach new audiences across Asia.

From China to Sydney

Yang joined the Flames earlier this year after building an impressive career in China.

The guard represented China at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, helping the country's 3x3 team win bronze. She was also part of the squad that won the 2023 Women's Asia Cup.

Fans cheer during the Sydney Flames' season opener, which drew a record opening-round crowd for the club. Source: Supplied

Speaking to SBS Mandarin, Yang said the move to Australia was driven by a desire to experience a different style of basketball.

"I've always wanted to play in different countries and experience different systems and styles of basketball," she said.

"I think that can help me improve."

Yang said she was already enjoying life in Sydney, both on and off the court.

"It feels great, and the weather is really nice. Everyone has been very kind to me, and I'm really looking forward to joining this big family."

'Already a star'

The excitement surrounding Yang's arrival was evident before she even stepped onto the court.

The Flames' season opener drew the largest opening-round crowd in club history, with many supporters telling SBS Mandarin they had come specifically to watch the Chinese star play.

"We're here to watch the Sydney Flames and support Yang Shuyu," one fan said.

"We hope she plays well and we hope she enjoys living in Sydney."

Yang Shuyu's growing fanbase was on display at the Flames' season opener. Source: Supplied

Another supporter said Yang had already become one of China's most recognisable basketballers.

"She's already a star in our national team," they said.

"We hope she can make her mark in an overseas league and show what she can do."

The attention Yang generated was matched by her performance.

She finished with 20 points, three rebounds and a steal, tying with teammate Jaz Shelley as the game's leading scorer in the Flames' 27-point win.

Flames coach Renae Garlepp said Yang had already made an impression despite only recently joining the squad.

"I think she played really well, and I'm happy for her," Garlepp said.

READ MORE How a South Sudanese Australian basketball star finally made it to the NBA

"What's great about her goes beyond the way she plays basketball. She's fitted into the team so easily.

"She's a lovely person and genuinely wants to be a good teammate. We're very lucky to have her."

Australian league sees rise in new Chinese fans

Yang's arrival also reflects a broader push by the WNBL to strengthen its connection with Chinese basketball fans.

She's one of four Chinese national team players competing in the league this season, alongside Southside Melbourne Flyers' Wang Siyu and Geelong Venom pair Zhang Wanglai and Han Xu.

WNBL chief operations officer Justin Nelson said the league had already seen growing interest from new audiences.

"Excitingly, we saw a huge rise in new fans, especially coming out to support the four Chinese national players and the high number of Opals playing this season," he said.

The Flames' season opener attracted a record opening-round crowd as the WNBL reported rising attendance and engagement. Source: Supplied

According to the league, opening-round attendance was up 40 per cent on last season, while social media engagement also reached record levels.

The growing interest comes as the WNBL expands its footprint in China. Last week, the league announced a broadcast partnership with Chinese media company YIDA that will make every game of the 2026-27 season available across Douyin, RedNote, Kuaishou and WeChat.

Nelson said the league hoped basketball could help build stronger connections between Australia and China.

"We hope basketball can serve as a bridge between the two countries, creating new opportunities for sporting exchange and new points of connection between Chinese and Australian cultures," he said.

Yang said she hopes to play a role in that exchange during her time in Australia.

"I'm really looking forward to meeting local fans and taking part in community events," she said.

"I also hope to bring some Chinese basketball culture here and build connections through sport."

title: A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry
text:
When energy provider Jemena announced on Wednesday that it had paused the installation of new 22-metre-tall concrete power poles needed for a nearby data centre, it triggered a chain reaction.

One of the country's biggest data centre operators, NEXTDC — which was forced to delay a planned expansion of its M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne — quickly saw its market valuation drop by around $3 billion.

The plunge was equivalent to about 42 per cent of the company's value, which could send fears through a surging sector still reeling from the failed float of one of its other biggest players.

Luke Laretive, CEO of Seneca Financial Solutions, said fear of "a significant downgrade" to NEXTDC's future earnings and a "contagion-type vibe" had spooked the share market.

"Are [data centre operators] going to be in a position now where ... despite having insatiable demand, they're unable to actually build these facilities in locations that have access to power, water, a community that's happy to have them nearby and are still close enough to the businesses and the people that want to use them?" the investment adviser told SBS' On The Money.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Some of the community around NEXTDC's West Footscray facility seemingly aren't happy to have it nearby. Local residents have previously expressed fears about the amount of diesel stored on the site and raised concerns about noise pollution.

The installation of the power poles required to meet the facility's significant electricity needs has also sparked community anger, with some residents of a nearby suburb using their cars and bins to block equipment deployed for the electricity network upgrade in September.

"Has NEXTDC lost its social licence to operate here, or have data centre providers more generally lost their social licence to operate?" Laretive asked.

Data centres and social licence

Less than two weeks earlier, data centre operator Firmus Technologies withdrew its application for public listing on the Australian Stock Exchange — a move that had been touted as the biggest since Telstra's 1997 float.

Firmus Technologies operates a data centre in Melbourne and is currently building another in Tasmania, with plans for at least two more — despite facing some community backlash.

A month before cancelling its public listing, Firmus announced several-year sponsorship deals with the Tasmania Devils AFL teams, Cricket Tasmania, and Tasmania JackJumpers and Jewels basketball teams, raising concerns of 'sportswashing'.

Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre (USSC), thinks the social licence for data centres could be in the process of being lost across Australia.

"The build-out has been incredibly fast and incredibly rapid," she said.

"And I think at the local level, communities are just feeling quite blindsided by all this development, and especially where it's happening on very large scale in areas where they're not used to this kind of development."

This sentiment conflicts with government messaging that, according to Shen, is more focused on a "narrative that these data centres are incredibly important public facilities for AI development".

That narrative may not be cutting through, with the USSC's 2025 annual poll finding that 67 per cent of Australians "want to prioritise the regulation of AI even at the cost of innovation".

"These Australians are basically saying that even if it slows innovation, we want to progress at a bit of a slower pace rather than having these technologies being shoved down our throats and being told that they're actually good for us," she said.

Some residents living near Next DC's M3 data centre in Melbourne's West Footscray have protested against the development. Source: AAP / Christopher Hopkins

However, Shen said people should be careful in making broad generalisations about the entire industry.

"Not all data centres are the same, not all of the technologies they use are the same from one operator to another, and the impact on the community really, really depends on the local conditions of that community," she said.

A data centre reliant on a polluting energy plant planning to build next to rural farmland used for cattle production will have a different impact to one hoping to build in a quiet suburb in the city.

Laretive, meanwhile, suggested data centre operators "learn from the likes of the BHP's and the Rio [Tinto]'s of the world" for community engagement.

"They are a real participant in the community, and they're not just there kind of soaking up resources," he said, referencing jobs created by mining companies.

Fears history is repeating itself

The Western Downs Digital Park is a $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland. AI giant Anthropic signed a lease for the first of four planned buildings, but the site has not yet received approval.

Luke Munn, an Australian Research Council future fellow with the University of Queensland, and Joanna Horton, a postdoctoral research fellow, are studying the proposed site.

"I think what we've seen in the last couple of years is a kind of increasing recognition from the public that there's an infrastructure and a material footprint around the AI boom," Munn said.

Horton said the community have been "really pushing back against the proposed development".

The proposed design for the Western Downs Digital Park. Source: Supplied / Urbis

A petition to stop the project already has 23,496 signatures — the most support for any active e-petition on the Queensland parliament website.

"It has been a hotspot for gas extraction, which has been a really big 'boom and bust' industry for the region," she said.

It's left residents concerned about history repeating, with new jobs being created only to disappear before too long. Another concern is natural resource extraction and water use, which critics have said could have a significant impact on the drought-prone region.

Horton said locals are also taking action, with the Environmental Defenders Office, a non-profit community legal centre, reporting a 250 per cent increase in inquiries related to data centres since January of this year.

Protesters gathered outside the Senate inquiry into data centre regulatory frameworks earlier this year. Source: AAP / James Ross

"I think that shows that all over Australia really are seeing data centres as a) something that they're not sure about that they have very real concerns about, and then b) something that they actually want to take action and push back on," she said.

Munn added that some companies now saw potential community opposition as a more important factor than geography or energy supply when choosing potential sites for data centres.

Is the data centre bubble starting to pop?

Shen doesn't think challenges faced by companies like Firmus are necessarily a sign that Australia's data centre boom is over, but she sees it as a warning that not every data centre company will see its investment pay off.

"There are firms jumping on this data centre bandwagon that are probably not going to be the best firms," she said.

"This is complex physical and digital infrastructure, and I don't think every single investor in a data centre is necessarily going to make their money back."

She says it could be a good thing if it encourages "more level-headedness with people investing in the right places".

Laretive said the NEXTDC case likely doesn't say too much about the demand for AI, but he still urges caution for investors.

"We need to be careful about evaluations and the amount of the future that we price into today's numbers and today's market capitalisation."

title: Meta pledges to 'defend ourselves vigorously' against Australian child harm lawsuit
text:
IN BRIEF A lawsuit is seeking compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were allegedly exposed to harmful content.

Meanwhile, a judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion for misleading consumers.

Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers.

The suit filed in the Federal Court on behalf of eight applicants seeks to recover compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media, law firm Minter Ellison and Litigation Lending said in a statement.

The Federal Court in Sydney issued a suppression order on Monday stopping publication of details of the claim and the identity of the applicants, court documents show.

"We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement.

Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who "would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia," Minter Ellison partner William Nolan said in a statement.

The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and big tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.7 billion (roughly $25 billion) in the United States to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users.

Meta ordered to pay US$25 billion in New Mexico

News of the Australian lawsuit came shortly after a judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay US$25 billion ($35.2 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in US President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent.

New Mexico attorney general Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against a company in US history.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.

Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.

In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said.

"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.

title: Flights will soon take off from Australia's newest airport. Here's where they're going
text:
In Brief Sydney's second airport opens on Sunday, offering 24-hour flights and new domestic and international routes.

Seven airlines have signed on, taking jetsetters to both domestic and international locations.

Sydney's second airport is about to open, marking the first new international airport built in Australia in more than 50 years.

Western Sydney International Airport, officially named Nancy-Bird Walton Airport, will welcome its first passengers on 25 October.

Located at Luddenham near Badgerys Creek, about 45km from Sydney's CBD, the airport is expected to reshape travel across Greater Sydney, offering an alternative to Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport and providing airlines access to a 24-hour aviation hub.

From flight routes and transport links to where it's located and how it differs from Sydney Airport, here's everything you need to know.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Where can you fly from Western Sydney International Airport?

Western Sydney International Airport will have one significant advantage over Sydney's existing airport: it can operate around the clock.

Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to an overnight curfew between 11pm and 6am, flights at the new airport can arrive and depart 24 hours a day.

That flexibility has helped attract domestic and international carriers, with seven airlines already committing to operate services from the airport.

Here's where they'll fly:

Qantas: Four weekly flights to Melbourne and Brisbane from March 2027.

Jetstar: Four weekly flights to the Gold Coast, three weekly flights to Brisbane, and daily services to Melbourne.

Qatar Airways: Three weekly flights to Doha's Hamad International Airport from 15 December, with additional services planned in coming years.

Air New Zealand: Three weekly flights to Auckland from 26 October.

Singapore Airlines: Daily flights to Singapore from 23 November.

Fiji Airways: Three weekly flights to Nadi.

Vietjet Air: Two weekly flights to Ho Chi Minh City from 10 January 2027, increasing to three in March 2027, plus four weekly flights to Bangkok via Vietjet Thailand.

Emirates has also been cleared to add seven weekly flights from the airport but is yet to announce a schedule.

Airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be announced as passenger numbers grow.

How do you get to Western Sydney International Airport?

One of the biggest questions facing travellers is how they will reach Sydney's newest airport.

Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is connected to Sydney's rail network, Western Sydney International Airport will initially rely on road connections and bus services while major transport infrastructure is completed.

A Sydney Metro line linking the airport with St Marys is under construction and expected to open next year.

Until then, passengers can connect to St Marys via a free airport shuttle bus, or travel by express coach, public bus, taxi, rideshare or private vehicle.

If you're driving, the airport is accessible via the new toll-free M12 Motorway and is about an hour from Sydney's CBD, depending on traffic conditions.

An express shuttle service will also connect the airport with Parramatta, Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport.

Current fares are:

Parramatta: $25 one way, $45 return.

Sydney CBD: $55 one way, $80 return.

Sydney Airport: $65 one way, $90 return.

From St Marys, passengers can connect to Sydney's wider rail network, though journeys to some parts of Sydney may take considerably longer than travelling via Kingsford Smith Airport.

State-run bus services will also link the airport with centres including Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown, Mount Druitt and Leppington.

For those driving, the airport has about 6,000 parking spaces available on site.

Where is Western Sydney International Airport?

Western Sydney International Airport is located at Luddenham, near Badgerys Creek, in Sydney's west.

The airport is approximately 45km from Sydney's CBD, 20km from Penrith and 15km from Liverpool.

It sits within the broader Western Sydney Aerotropolis precinct and will become Sydney's second major airport when passenger operations begin on Sunday.

Why is Western Sydney International Airport a big deal?

Plans for a second major Sydney airport have been debated for decades as governments looked for ways to meet the city's growing aviation demand.

The airport is expected to become the centrepiece of the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, a major business and infrastructure precinct that planners hope will drive jobs, investment and development across the region.

When it opens, Western Sydney International Airport will be able to handle up to 10 million passengers a year.

That capacity is expected to expand significantly over coming decades, with airport operators forecasting it could eventually handle 82 million passengers annually.

While flight options will initially be limited, airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be added as the airport grows.

Will Western Sydney International Airport make airfares cheaper?

Aviation experts have previously told SBS News that the change will fundamentally alter the country's airfare market and could drive prices down for consumers by opening up air travel capacity.

However with rail links that may not be ready until 2028, getting to the airport could theoretically incur a cost that would be similar or more than the savings on a ticket.

text:

As the new airport opens in western Sydney, we take a look at how it became a reality. See all stories .

Once Western Sydney International Airport opens on Sunday, the true strength of demand for flights from Australia’s newest airport will start to show. But success won’t happen overnight, aviation experts say. The curfew-free airport is expected to benefit from Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport’s limits on capacity. But its growth may be held back by passengers’ unwillingness to try the new hub some 50 kilometres away from Sydney’s CBD, as well as airlines’ reluctance to fly there. How busy will it get? An artist’s render of Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport. Australia’s first newly built airport in more than half a century is launching at a time of spiralling costs for airlines amid surging fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East, and the kind of global uncertainty that makes market predictions difficult. But playing in its favour are Sydney Airport’s well-known issues with capacity, which are often worsened by its air traffic control staffing issues, inclement coastal weather conditions and a strict curfew, which prevents night take-offs and landings.

Advertisement

With those conflicting factors, it’s perhaps not surprising that only seven airlines have committed to fly out of WSI so far, averaging about six return flights a day, domestic and international routes combined. Sydney Airport, by contrast, is at near capacity with about 400 return flights a day across almost 60 airlines. ‘Many big cities globally have two or more commercial airports. It was absolutely necessary here as well.’ Former IATA business strategist Tony Laverghetta Qatar Airways finally committed to flying to WSI this week, though not before late 2027. With crude oil at more than $US100 a barrel, airlines can’t afford to fly uneconomical routes. High costs and a shortfall of new airframes have limited the availability of planes and pilots. Perhaps for this reason, Qantas will run only four return flights per week to Brisbane and four flights per week to Melbourne when it starts to fly from WSI on March 28, 2027, using 95-seat QantasLink Embraer E190 aircraft. Air New Zealand will fly three times weekly to WSI from Auckland.

Advertisement

After that, it depends on how well things go. Senior aviation consultant Ian Guy says that if airlines make more money off their routes at WSI than elsewhere, they’ll stick with it. But if the routes are unprofitable, after a season or a couple of years they’ll to pull the flights. ‘Slow burn’ A look overseas offers examples of the dynamics starting to play out at WSI. Secondary airports operating far from the city centres they nominally serve, tend to attract low-cost airlines that effectively “plant a flag” to watch the demand, says Guy, who is a director at Melbourne-based Tango 5 aviation consultancy. A carrier can then quickly scale up if demand supports it. Qantas-owned Jetstar has made the biggest commitment to WSI so far. Jetstar will fly up to 24 return services a week from Western Sydney, with up to 14 to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast, and three a week to Brisbane.

Advertisement

Vietnam-based low-cost carrier Vietjet will start flying two return services a week to Ho Chi Minh City in January. The airline’s stablemate Vietjet Thailand is expected to begin flying four times a week to Bangkok in November 2027. In addition to Air New Zealand’s commitment, Singapore Airlines will have one daily return flight from WSI to Singapore Changi. Related Article Aviation 80 years in the making: How Sydney’s new international airport finally took off Behind the scenes, subsidies for operational fees are also a factor. A $16 million Western Sydney International Take-Off Fund backed jointly by the airport and the NSW state government has been designed to help woo airlines to the new airport. Yet what happens after the initial sweetener is a different matter, Guy says, and it’s possible that “once that subsidy falls away, the route doesn’t have the same economics and so it stops existing.”

Advertisement

Ellis Taylor, Asia editor for aviation analytics company Cirium, expects the new airport uptake would be “a bit of a slower burn” but WSI’s ability to operate late at night and early in the morning adds “an interesting dynamic”. ‘More than just the poor man’s Sydney Airport’ WSI is “more than just the poor man’s Sydney Airport,” Taylor says, comparing its premise with when Jetstar began flying from Avalon in 2004. “It’s not really sort of seen as an alternative to the main airport as yet. It’s more about opening up an additional demand point,” she says. And once that is done, the airport’s viability in the larger aviation market will be tested. Yet, in other ways, WSI and Avalon could not be more different. While WSI is built on the expectation of expanding commercial flights to Sydney’s west, Avalon was built in the 1950s for use by military planes and only turned into a commercial airport in the 1990s. A view from the new airport’s top floor, where international passengers will arrive. Sitthixay Ditthavong

Advertisement

Melbourne Tullamarine, Victoria’s primary airport, has plenty of capacity, hosts more than 40 airlines (including, from this month, Finnair) and operates without a curfew. Avalon is operating against an unconstrained competitor. In turn, it has sought to specialise and tap the growing logistics and freight sectors to link Victoria to export markets in the Middle East. The proximity of airports often shape where airlines base themselves. In London, Heathrow is the premium airport, serving alongside smaller airports Gatwick, Stansted and Luton, which function as hubs for low-cost carriers such as easyJet, Ryanair, and Wizz Air. Related Article Aviation Qatar Airways plans flights to western Sydney from late 2027 “If you really looked at the density of their flight operations...they have each picked particular airports to focus on,” says Guy. A UK-based network planner with knowledge of the Australian market believes WSI will be a success, as it adds real international capacity to the city.

Advertisement

“It relieves Sydney’s peak-slot scarcity and it’s curfew-free, so carriers can build in the late-night and early morning departures that make European connections work” – a big advantage over Kingsford Smith, she points out. Western Sydney is also “a big, multicultural catchment with strong VFR [visiting friends and relatives] demand and family ties abroad”.WSI will target the leisure and visiting friends and relatives market, which is cheaper, volume-led, she says, “while Kingsford Smith holds the premium end”. The VFR market has its own dynamic. People typically take fewer trips, but travel in bigger groups. They tend to fly on less expensive fares, too, and have more luggage. This could be a positive for WSI’s launch, as passengers are likely to travel by car and won’t be dissuaded by WSI’s nascent ground transportation. Escalators and stairs link a bag-drop area to departures on the first level. Sitthixay Ditthavong VFR represents a significant plank of the aviation market in Australia. NSW Premier Chris Minns has been courting India as a major source of visitors to the state. But demographics don’t mean an automatic embrace from homeland airlines.

Advertisement

In a media presentation early this month by Air India head of global sales Manish Puri played down the possibility of serving WSI for now, saying that while the “options of opening new stations always remain… initially, our intention is to densify our current network” with more frequencies. About 60 per cent of Air India traffic to and from Australia is VFR, Puri says, and while VFR will remain a “strong point” for the airline, Air India wants to move more into meeting demand for travel to Europe. The addition of WSI to Australia’s network of airports could spur other changes too. Loading Perth-based senior aviation consultant Bill Meeke says the combination of the curfew at Sydney Airport and the three-hour time zone difference with Western Australia during daylight saving means that “the daily window of access for flights from Perth is very narrow for much of the year”. Curfew-free flights at WSI could change that.

Advertisement

As the new airport finds its place in the national aviation grid, it may spur other opportunities. It’s possible an overseas carrier would make WSI a stopover between a domestic airport and an international destination to pick up enough passengers to make its flight profitable. There could be a route like Cairns-Western Sydney-Hong Kong, for example, where passengers from two domestic points are used to fill the plane. Related Article Aviation How chook farm spurred Paul Keating’s push for new airport at Badgerys Creek Once WSI kicks into gear and proves a business success for the first airlines, it could become a meaningful competitor to Sydney Airport and force the city’s long-established hub to lift its game, says Guy. Unable to add a lot more airlines, Sydney Airport will then have to help carriers up-gauge their aircraft, accommodating larger-capacity, bigger planes, he says. But that’s in the future. “I suspect at the moment they’re not overly worried.”

Tony Laverghetta, a former International Air Transport Association business strategist, says it will take time, but eventually WSI “will become a solid option for travellers”, especially when its new metro line opens. “Many big cities globally have two or more commercial airports,” Laverghetta says, pointing to London, New York, Milan and Paris. “It was absolutely necessary here as well.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. title: This genre-bending novel blends mystery, romance and art history
text:
Gates’ fiction is often hilarious and tongue-in-cheek, especially when he relays his unreliable narrator’s penchant for mansplaining thesis ideas to anyone who will (or won’t) listen, including bartenders and sunbaking Dutch tourists. The reader can occasionally feel like someone trapped on an aeroplane next to a passenger who won’t stop talking. Gates is well aware of this, though, and introduces a wonderful parallel narrative where Tiffen falls in love with Agnés, who he meets staring at a painting in a Sydney art gallery. From Barcelona, she works at the Berowra Waters Inn, and Tiffen encircles her in a bid to win her affections; he desperately needs a muse.

Playing detective is Christopher Tiffen, a PhD student writing an art history thesis and scrambling for clues on what happened to Wake: Did he go to prison during the Spanish Civil War? Where have his artworks gone? Is he still alive? Any PhD student in writing and literature or art history researcher will get a kick out of Gates’ blurring of genres and Tiffen’s hapless and fantasist attempts to fit his findings into academic parameters when he really wants to explode the narrative. Art lovers will see pointers everywhere to artworks and painters, as Tiffen recognises the brushstrokes of places he visits.

Roaming between Sydney and Hydra, Hill End and Barcelona, London and Paris, Geoffrey Gates’ third novel, The Phantom Surrealist , is a playful search for an elusive Australian artist, Robert J Wake, who grows up on the gritty streets of Surry Hills and ends up on surrealist shores with Miro and Picasso. Soon after, he disappears in Spain.

This contemporary narrative cleverly echoes Wake’s journey: Wake sailed to pre-World War II London while Tiffen flies into Heathrow; Tiffen works alone in a Kombi Van in Hill End, where Wake painted in an abandoned cottage. Eventually, the narratives have to intersect, and they do in a deus ex machina that seems too insanely neat, but perhaps not for the imaginings of Tiffen; he is searching for “the uncomfortable depths where the fluid truth lies”, after all.

Gates’ central exploration is of fantasy and escape, fakery and the false motivations we project onto others – who we know and who we imagine we know – the stories we make to fill in the gaps when there are no answers. Tiffen is like a phantom in his own life, too, curiously lacking self-awareness. At times the interplay between the parallel narratives seems too delineated. Perhaps more blurring of lines between character, time and space would have kept it aptly surreal and uncertain.

Ultimately, the book is an examination of what tends to fall through the cracks. The painters’ women-lovers who meld into the muse landscape rather than being recognised for their own work and activism. The pre/postwar Australian artists who leave our shores to become key figures in international art scenes but don’t exist in the galleries, catalogues and archives. It’s no surprise that Wake works in the propaganda unit in Spain and the camouflage unit in Australia – where his work is transitory and has no signature. Even Hill End, once thriving but now abandoned, has become the “land of disappearance”.

The Phantom Surrealist is an enticing novel that dissects the narrative of what it means to be an Australian artist like Robert J Wake in the world, and what it takes to find a sense of home. Caught in the tension between knowing everything about art, and not able to express himself as an artist, Tiffen has to make do with losing himself in the imagined lives of others. Gates threads these two characters’ worlds together skilfully, shaping a mysterious ficto-biography of artistic grandeur, that also manages to have a lot of fun along the way.

And I think I have confidence in the first-class system. I have confidence in the next man in being an experienced 32-year-old like a Jake Weatherald or Pete Handscomb, Kurtis Patterson, who have all done well. “I think right now it’s that we’ve got a strong Australian cricket team. We haven’t played very well, and people will doubt that over this week. They doubt if it’s a strong cricket team. It has been [strong] over a period of time. We’ve had a shit week. That’s OK. Past selections show that we’re trying to slot guys in to continue to be world No.1.” Nevertheless, Head joined captain Pat Cummins in accepting that batting performances had to improve if the team was to succeed in Cape Town. “It’s difficult putting the finger on things,” he said. “I think we’ve spoken as a group going into the series that we’ve sort of had one individual each time, and they’ve always been different individuals, and we sort of haven’t been able to get that collective batting day that we would desire as a team.

“So if you look through it, or you look Greeny [Cameron Green] and Darwin, in Mackay we batted once and 180 was enough for two innings. Then you look at last week with Renners’ [Matt Renshaw] game. Again this game, I was able to step up and get runs, but like it’s always been sort of one individual at a time, and we haven’t been able to get that collective. And we talked about that into the series. “We just haven’t been able to find that, and it’s something that the team’s been really good at over a long period of time now is that built big partnerships, substantial partnerships that win games of cricket. We just haven’t been able to find that in the last couple of months. It’s very hard to put a finger on while we’re playing some exceptional attacks in some trying conditions. But yeah, it’s not through lack of trying.” Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne reacts as he bats on day four. AP Photo The players will rest up ahead of the Newlands Test, with some partners and families arriving for the final week of the tour. Head said it was important to keep the series ledger in perspective and not let the St George’s Park performance “eat away” at them. “I think it’s pretty clear on what we got wrong,” he said. “We had a pretty shithouse day. As simple as that. If we don’t get bowled out for 99, more than likely the Test goes to a draw. It’s pretty obvious what we did poorly.

We’ll talk about it over the next few days. We have a couple of training sessions. Guys will be switched on. Guys will be ready to go again. “ It’s not lost on us, but you’ve got to dust yourself off pretty quickly because you’re in the series. And if you let that eat away at you, then you start slowly next week, and we could end up with another game at this point in a week.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday. Dual international Lote Tuqiri says rugby officials have erred by leaving Zac Lomax out of Australia A’s side to play the United States and believes fellow code-hopper Mark Nawaqanitawase has shown courage by considering a switch to Italy or Fiji for the World Cup. “I like the fact he’s got the balls to stand on 10 toes and do what he’s doing,” Tuqiri said of Nawaqanitawase. Mark Nawaqanitawase says he hasn’t made up his mind on who he wants to play for at the 2027 Rugby World Cup. Getty Images If anyone knows how Nawaqanitawase is feeling, it’s Tuqiri. Tuqiri played three Tests for Fiji in 2000, before switching allegiances to the Kangaroos.

Advertisement

And after a successful stint in rugby union finished in 2009, the winger played another four Tests for the Kangaroos in 2010 before returning to Fiji in 2014. “There’s a calling for it,” he said. Lote Tuqiri played for Australia and Fiji in rugby league, as well as well as two World Cups for the Wallabies. Tim Clayton “I know it’s hard to fathom when you’ve played in a different jersey. It’s more so the pride it gives you; it makes you puff out your chest. “Whether it’s now, whether it’s down the track, it’s going to happen.”

Advertisement

Another perspective Opinion

Wallabies Mark, we fancy you as the Messiah. Don’t be a naughty boy Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Nawaqanitawase’s decision not to immediately pledge his allegiance to the Wallabies has caused a stir, including among former players. “As a proud Wallaby and a proud Australian, I want people that want to play for our country to play for our country,” 103-Test Wallaby Matt Giteau said on the KOKO podcast. Tuqiri said he understood the mixed sentiment toward Nawaqanitawase’s decision to not yet reveal his intentions. “He hasn’t made up his mind yet, has he? He should be given the time to do that,” Tuqiri said.

Advertisement

Although Rugby Australia are keen on selecting him for the Wallabies, former coach Joe Schmidt didn’t pick him in mid-2024 after he signed with the Sydney Roosters. Nawaqanitawase was eventually selected for Australia’s Olympic Sevens side, but the earlier decision to leave him out caused a stir. Mark Nawaqanitawase in action for the Waratahs in 2023. Getty Meanwhile, NRL boss Peter V’landys has showered Nawaqanitawase with praise, making it clear he wants to lure him back after his two-year deal with the Wild Knights in Japan. Tuqiri said he thought Rugby Australia needed to do more to put their arms around players, even when players chose to leave Super Rugby.

Advertisement

“I don’t think we do enough,” he said. “I reckon he’s probably got a bad taste in his mouth from the last time he put on the rugby jersey. I couldn’t believe when he wasn’t getting picked for the Tahs. I was like, ‘Why is this kid on the bench?’ I know he was young, but I was gobsmacked that he wasn’t in the 23 at times.” With Nawaqanitawase’s Wallabies future not clear, Tuqiri said he was surprised former NSW Blues Origin flyer Lomax wasn’t more in the frame for the Wallabies. “You’d think you’d give him a crack,” Tuqiri said. “But just from an outside looking in, just give him a go.” Lomax, who will join the PNG Chiefs in 2028, was a late addition to the Australia A squad last week but wasn’t picked for the first of two matches starting in Nashville on Sunday against the Eagles.

Advertisement

Instead, Stephen Larkham selected Wallaby Dylan Pietsch and rising Queenslander flyer Tim Ryan on the wing. Lomax scored twice for the Force across seven matches for the Super Rugby side, but a groin issue kept him out of the frame for the home international season. Zac Lomax has made a promising start to his rugby career at the Western Force. Getty Images Tuqiri said he had been impressed by Lomax’s initial move into the XV-man game and couldn’t understand why he wasn’t starting for Australia A. “You can’t give away Test jerseys, but Australia A is a mechanism to test players out,” he said. “It’s a development team and this guy’s a part of your development.

Advertisement

“And as every athlete knows, you learn the most on the field, not training. It’s the wins and losses and how you navigate yourself on game day. “I think you start him on the wing. I don’t think you do a Suaalii (Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii) and put him in 13 or whatever. Lote Tuqiri says Zac Lomax (L) needs to play on the wing for Australia A, and not in the centres like fellow league recruit, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (right). Getty Images “You’ve only got him for 12 months. We’ve got to pick your best team and you’ve got to give him a chance to put his hand up because you know what he can offer.” Meanwhile, Australia A prop Tom Robertson said the touring party was enjoying the “once in a lifetime opportunity” to play in Nashville, but were eager to impress to push for Test selection, especially with the World Cup less than 12 months away.

Advertisement

“It definitely adds another layer of importance and meaning to the tour,” he said. The USA will host the 2031 World Cup and World Rugby is intent on bringing as many games to the continent as possible to build momentum. Asked whether their arrival had been recognised by locals, Robertson, the 39-Test Wallaby, said they had been copping plenty of questions around protection equipment. “Yeah, definitely. They either say rugby or wrestling when you get in the elevators and going down the streets,” he said. “Normally there’s a bit of laughter when you tell them it’s rugby not wrestling. They’re getting into their rugby. Nashville’s definitely trying to push the rugby scene here ahead of the World Cup, which is awesome.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday. A controversial train timetable shake-up that would have affected up to a quarter of Sydney Train commuters has been abandoned following public backlash. NSW Premier Chris Minns on Saturday revealed the government’s dramatic U-turn on planned changes to the T4, T8 and South Coast lines’ timetables, which were scheduled to commence on November 15. The Minns government has abandoned controversial changes to train timetables. Dominic Lorrimer The decision was made “following feedback from commuters and local communities”. The changes – which the government had pledged would deliver more frequent services and additional capacity across southern Sydney and the South Coast – would have resulted in longer commute times for some passengers.

Advertisement

Those travelling on the T4 between Waterfall and the central city, for example, were facing trip times of up to 14 minutes longer because of extra stops. Passengers travelling from Heathcote, Engadine and Loftus stations would also have seen trip times to the city increase by about 12 minutes in the morning peak and about 14 minutes in the evening peak. South Coast passengers travelling to Sydney Airport from Wollongong would have had to go all the way to Central and double-back on the T8 if they wished to avoid switching twice at stations on their journey. All trains on the South Coast line were scheduled to terminate at Central. Some services on the T4 and T8 lines would have increased in frequency. Minns said commuters wanted a reliable service that could get them to work and home on time. “We’ve listened to commuters and local MPs, and we’re not proceeding with these timetable changes,” he said. “Our priority is fixing reliability and giving passengers a railway they can depend on.”

Advertisement

Transport Minister John Graham said public response to the timetable changes had prompted “the decision that we have more to do to invest in reliability first”. Related Article Updated

Sydney Metro Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line The existing timetable will now remain in place, with the government saying it will turn its focus to improving reliability on the ageing network, parts of which are more than 100 years old. Transport for NSW will also engage “with communities on future service improvements”. Most of the proposed timetable changes were to the T4 Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra, and the South Coast lines, which between them carry about 250,000 passengers a day, or a quarter of Sydney Trains’ patronage. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
